extraction.name: HELVIPAD
extraction.description: HELVIPAD is a real-world dataset for omnidirectional stereo depth estimation, featuring 40K video frames from video sequences across diverse environments, including crowded indoor and outdoor scenes with various lighting conditions. Collected using two 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup and a LiDAR sensor, the dataset includes accurate depth and disparity labels by projecting 3D point clouds onto equirectangular images. Additionally, an augmented training set with increased label density is provided using depth completion.
extraction.creator: Mehdi Zayene, Jannik Endres, Albias Havolli, Charles Corbière, Salim Cherkaoui, Alexandre Kontouli, Alexandre Alahi (EPFL, Switzerland; TU Darmstadt, Germany)
extraction.citeAs: Zayene, M., Endres, J., Havolli, A., Corbière, C., Cherkaoui, S., Kontouli, A., & Alahi, A. (2024). HELVIPAD: A Real-World Dataset for Omnidirectional Stereo Depth Estimation. arXiv:2411.18335.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data were collected using a custom-built rig equipped with two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup with a 19.1 cm baseline, capturing equirectangular images at 30 fps, paired with an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor with a vertical field of view of 42.4°, operating at 10 fps, and mounted 45.0 cm below the bottom camera. A central processor manages data capture and ensures device synchronization. Data were collected across distinct scenes encompassing indoor (e.g., corridors, halls) and outdoor (e.g., squares, external parking, footpaths) settings in various lighting conditions on a university campus. In total, 29 video sequences were collected.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Ground-truth depth labels cover only a fraction of the total pixels due to the sparse nature of LiDAR point clouds compared to high-resolution camera images. The original ratio of labeled pixels is approximately 12%, which is increased to 61% after depth completion. Sky areas and regions with insufficient nearby measurements are excluded from labeling.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of paired equirectangular images from two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras (top-bottom configuration) and synchronized LiDAR point clouds from an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor, collected across indoor and outdoor scenes on a university campus. The cameras capture images at 30 fps with an initial resolution of 3840×1920 pixels; the LiDAR operates at 10 fps with 64 beams.
extraction.rai:dataImputationProtocol: A fully automated depth completion pipeline tailored for 360° images was developed. The pipeline uses temporal aggregation of point clouds (current frame plus four preceding and four succeeding frames), interpolates depth on spherical grid points using a weighted average of k-nearest neighbors (k=17), and applies filtering to exclude points with high uncertainty (relative weighted variance threshold) or lacking nearby measurements (out-of-distribution threshold of ~0.37°). The ratio of interpolated points (RIP) is set to 0.8. This increases labeled pixel ratio from ~12% to ~61%.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: LiDAR point clouds are projected onto equirectangular images via an optimized rotation and translation transformation (minimizing pixel error using BFGS optimization). Spherical disparity is computed from depth values using the angular difference formula. After cropping unnecessary regions (sky, ground), images are downsized from a width of 1024 pixels to 512. To match the LiDAR's frame rate (10 fps), one out of every three camera frames is retained. Hardware-triggered synchronization using an external flash is used to align camera and LiDAR data streams.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: After LiDAR-to-image mapping and depth completion, unnecessary regions (sky, ground) are cropped from images. Images are downsized from a width of 1024 pixels to 512 to enable more efficient training. The resulting dataset comprises 39,553 paired images with corresponding depth and disparity maps at a resolution of 1920×512 pixels. The dataset is split into train-val (20 sequences, 29,407 frames) and test sets (6 sequences, 10,146 frames), ensuring proportional representation of outdoor, indoor, and night outdoor sequences. Each test sequence was manually reviewed to ensure no overlap of scenes or areas with the train set.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Depth and disparity labels are generated by projecting 3D LiDAR point clouds onto equirectangular images. The LiDAR-to-image mapping is optimized by minimizing the error between projected points and their corresponding locations on equirectangular images using BFGS optimization. Disparity values are derived from depth values using the spherical disparity formula. An augmented training set with increased label density is produced using the depth completion pipeline.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Alignment accuracy was assessed by calculating pixel error using Euclidean distances between 200 randomly selected LiDAR points and their image positions, resulting in an average error of 1.7 pixels. For visually challenging areas (e.g., object edges), the error remains at 8.0 pixels. The overall average pixel error across the dataset is 8.0 pixels (relative error of 0.40% of the image diagonal). Depth completion quality was validated by splitting each LiDAR point cloud into training and test sets and computing depth estimation metrics on the test set.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset captures dynamic human environments with pedestrians present in scenes. An average of 13.33 pedestrians appear in indoor sequences and 17.65 pedestrians in outdoor sequences.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to support the development of mobile robots for real-world applications such as autonomous driving, healthcare, and agriculture, where accurate 3D representations of dynamic human environments are crucial for navigation and interaction.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset was collected on a university campus, which may limit generalization to other environments. The depth completion algorithm increases the density of low-range depth values (particularly within the 0–10 meter range), enriching the representation of closer objects. Indoor sequences exhibit a more rapid decline in pixel percentage beyond 10 meters compared to outdoor sequences. The temporal aggregation approach may introduce errors for fast-moving objects like cars.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset was collected on a university campus, so while it captures common urban environments, it may not fully represent all real-world scenarios. The depth completion approach is limited for fast-moving objects like cars due to the temporal aggregation window. Occlusions between the LiDAR and cameras were not explicitly handled. The LiDAR's vertical field of view (42.4°) limits the region of the image that can be labeled. Depth completion does not provide labels for pixels at object boundaries.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing of omnidirectional stereo depth estimation models. Benchmarking stereo depth estimation approaches for both standard and omnidirectional images. The dataset serves as a testbed for assessing robustness of depth estimation methods to diverse lighting conditions and depth ranges, and for cross-dataset generalization studies.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor for depth measurement; BFGS optimization algorithm for LiDAR-to-image mapping; custom depth completion pipeline using temporal aggregation and k-nearest neighbor interpolation; KISS-ICP for LiDAR odometry estimation
